Other bacterial targets (Escherichia coli K1, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus agalactiae, Streptococcus pneumoniae), viral targets (CMV, enterovirus, HSV-1, HSV-2, HHV-6, human parechovirus, VZV) and Cryptococcus: not detected

alternatives: Co-trimoxazole for Listeria only with a genuine penicillin allergy (not the case here), and never with methotrexate continued
Meropenem 2 g IV every 8 hours (covers Listeria) if a beta-lactam hypersensitivity limits ampicillin
interactions: Ampicillin (and other penicillins) + methotrexate: reduced renal tubular secretion of methotrexate raises its levels and toxicity (myelosuppression, mucositis, hepatotoxicity), more so with reduced kidney function.
Co-trimoxazole + methotrexate: additive antifolate effect with risk of severe pancytopenia.

Dexamethasone + prednisone: duplicate glucocorticoid; prednisone can be held while dexamethasone is given, but after 4 years of prednisone the adrenal axis is suppressed, so glucocorticoid cover must continue when dexamethasone stops.
Ampicillin: renally cleared; review the dose interval against creatinine clearance (eGFR about 42).
Gentamicin, if added for synergy: nephrotoxic at eGFR about 42; use only with levels and daily creatinine.
Levothyroxine, alendronate, calcium carbonate and omeprazole: no clinically significant interaction with ceftriaxone, ampicillin or dexamethasone.
output.proposed: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours + ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours + dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours. Current medicines: prednisone 7.5 mg daily (4 years), methotrexate 15 mg weekly, folic acid 1 mg daily, alendronate 70 mg weekly, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, calcium carbonate 600 mg twice daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily. No known drug allergies. Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (baseline 1.1; eGFR about 42 mL/min/1.73m2, CKD-EPI 2021).
warnings: Hold methotrexate during the acute illness; establish when the last weekly dose was taken; monitor blood counts, creatinine and liver tests.
Do not stop glucocorticoid cover abruptly: resume prednisone when dexamethasone is stopped, with stress-dose cover during sepsis.
If vancomycin is added: dose by weight with AUC-guided monitoring and daily creatinine.

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT rely on ceftriaxone alone to cover Listeria monocytogenes: Listeria is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins; ampicillin is required.
Do NOT delay empiric ampicillin-inclusive antibiotic therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.

Do not delay lumbar puncture or antibiotics to obtain a CT head: cranial imaging is not routine before lumbar puncture (WHO 2025 Annex A.4; NICE NG240 1.4.6) and no imaging-first criterion is present.
Do NOT attribute the CSF pleocytosis to methotrexate-associated aseptic meningitis: Gram-positive rods, a glucose ratio of 0.20 and Listeria monocytogenes on PCR establish bacterial meningitis.
Do NOT continue methotrexate during the acute illness.
Do not continue adjunctive dexamethasone after Listeria monocytogenes is identified.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).

Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of age over 60 (78 years) and immunosuppression (prednisone 7.5 mg daily and methotrexate 15 mg weekly) (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.6.6).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Stop dexamethasone on identification of Listeria monocytogenes (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 Annex A.4 criterion is present (GCS 12, no focal signs, no new cranial nerve deficit (the reduced hearing is longstanding presbycusis), no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised: prednisone 7.5 mg daily with weekly methotrexate). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose with paired serum glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, CSF lactate) at LP.

Hold methotrexate during the acute illness: ampicillin reduces its renal clearance, kidney function is reduced (creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, eGFR about 42) and infection is active; monitor blood counts, creatinine and liver tests, and restart only after recovery.

Continue glucocorticoid cover after 4 years of prednisone: prednisone may be held while dexamethasone is given, but resume it when dexamethasone is stopped, with stress-dose cover during sepsis; do not leave her without a glucocorticoid.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes (ampicillin MIC 0.12 mcg/mL), with the interval reviewed against creatinine clearance; stop ceftriaxone; 21 days in total (NICE NG240).
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, and within 4 weeks of being well enough to test (NICE NG240).

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis; no cardiac arrhythmia indication in this case.
No clinical features of infective endocarditis as a primary source; echocardiography is not part of routine bacterial meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or management.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis; CT and MRI cover all relevant indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

CT before lumbar puncture is not indicated: no WHO 2025 Annex A.4 criterion is present (GCS 12, no focal signs, no new cranial nerve deficit (the reduced hearing is longstanding presbycusis), no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised: prednisone 7.5 mg daily with weekly methotrexate). Imaging here only delays the lumbar puncture.

accepted: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Listeria monocytogenes

differential.key_features: The commonest cause in older adults and the target of the empirical ceftriaxone and dexamethasone; excluded: S. pneumoniae not detected on the panel, Gram-positive rods (not diplococci), Listeria in blood and CSF.
Excluded: 940 cells/microL with 82% neutrophils, glucose ratio 0.20, protein 342 mg/dL, viral panel targets not detected.
Confusion in an older adult raises it; excluded: no focal signs or seizures, HSV-1 and HSV-2 not detected on the panel, bacterial CSF with Listeria.
Immunosuppression raises the risk, but onset is over 48 hours with a neutrophilic CSF and an identified organism.
Possible on long-term immunosuppression; excluded: acute neutrophilic CSF, Cryptococcus not detected on the panel.
Described mainly after intrathecal or high-dose methotrexate, not low-dose weekly oral therapy; excluded: glucose ratio 0.20, Gram-positive rods and Listeria on PCR and in blood cultures.

key_clinical_evidence: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis predominantly affects adults over 60 and immunocompromised patients, including those on corticosteroids or disease-modifying agents; this patient meets both criteria.

Dietary exposure to unpasteurised soft cheese is the classic risk factor for Listeria acquisition; the history of such exposure three weeks prior is temporally consistent with incubation and presentation.

Listeria is uniformly resistant to cephalosporins; failure to include ampicillin in the empirical regimen would leave the causative organism uncovered despite an otherwise appropriate ceftriaxone backbone.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

The CSF pattern (neutrophilic pleocytosis, glucose ratio 0.20, markedly raised protein, Gram-positive rods on Gram stain) is bacterial; Listeria monocytogenes on the CSF multiplex panel and in blood cultures establishes the organism. The Gram stain shows rods in only about a third of Listeria cases (Brouwer 2012), so a negative stain would not have excluded it.

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 Annex A.4 criterion is present (GCS 12, no focal signs, no new cranial nerve deficit (the reduced hearing is longstanding presbycusis), no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised: prednisone 7.5 mg daily with weekly methotrexate). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

Methotrexate-associated aseptic meningitis is described mainly after intrathecal or high-dose methotrexate, not low-dose weekly oral therapy; drug-induced aseptic meningitis gives a sterile CSF with a normal glucose, whereas this CSF has a glucose ratio of 0.20, Gram-positive rods and Listeria on PCR.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Methotrexate-associated aseptic meningitis is described mainly after intrathecal or high-dose methotrexate, not low-dose weekly oral therapy, and drug-induced aseptic meningitis gives a sterile CSF with a normal glucose; this CSF has a glucose ratio of 0.20, Gram-positive rods and Listeria on PCR.
red_herrings.data_point: Methotrexate in the medication list as a potential cause of drug-induced aseptic meningitis
red_herrings.intended_effect: An agent anchored on the medication list might consider drug-induced aseptic meningitis from methotrexate and underweight the bacterial diagnosis, potentially delaying empiric antibiotics.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A week of mild nasal congestion does not explain fever to 39.1, meningism and a fall in consciousness over 48 hours; a viral attribution must not delay lumbar puncture and antibiotics. Ampicillin cover is driven by age and immunosuppression, not by the upper respiratory symptoms.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on a viral illness or sinusitis and delay the meningitis work-up.

labs.interpretation: Leukocytosis (WBC 18.4 x10^9/L, 82% neutrophils, 8% bands). Mild normocytic anemia (Hb 11.6 g/dL). Hyponatremia (Na 130 mEq/L). Mildly elevated creatinine (1.3 mg/dL) from baseline. Elevated glucose (112 mg/dL). Markedly elevated CRP (164 mg/L), procalcitonin (6.8 ng/mL), ESR (88 mm/hr), and lactate (2.9 mmol/L). Mildly elevated ALT (52 U/L). TSH within normal limits. Coagulation studies normal. Albumin normal. HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody non-reactive.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward: classic presentation with fever, headache, meningismus, altered mental status, positive Gram stain and culture. The key discriminating feature — Listeria's cephalosporin resistance requiring ampicillin — is directly readable from the CSF/culture data and the clinical context of age over 60 and immunosuppression. Red herring (methotrexate as drug-induced aseptic meningitis cause) is easily dismissed by the CSF neutrophilic pattern and positive Gram stain.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 4 required tools (labs, blood cultures, CSF, drug interactions), 2 red herrings, single diagnostic chain; no CT before LP (no WHO 2025 Annex A.4 criterion)
metadata.real_seed_note: Demographics and organism loosely based on: Mancini I et al. 'A Case of Listeria monocytogenes ST-219 Meningo-Encephalitis.' Front Microbiol. 2019;9:3121. PMC6339192. CC-BY 4.0. The real case was an 83-year-old Italian woman with blood and CSF culture-confirmed Listeria monocytogenes meningitis. Case demographics were adapted (age adjusted to 78, Italian-American ethnicity, rheumatoid arthritis immunosuppression added for clinical authenticity); clinical values were constructed de novo for the benchmark.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Carmela Esposito is a 78-year-old right-handed retired schoolteacher with rheumatoid arthritis on low-dose prednisone and methotrexate who was brought to the emergency department by her daughter after 48 hours of worsening confusion, high fever, and neck stiffness. Her daughter reports that two days ago, Mrs. Esposito called complaining of a severe, rapidly worsening diffuse headache and generalised malaise. Her temperature at home was 38.4 degrees Celsius. The daughter gave her acetaminophen 1000 mg and attributed the symptoms to a possible viral illness given mild nasal congestion the patient had noted over the preceding week. Overnight, the patient's confusion worsened markedly. This morning, her daughter found her lying in bed, unable to recognise her, not knowing what year it was, and complaining bitterly of photophobia and neck pain. She was unable to stand without assistance. The daughter also reports that Mrs. Esposito has a history of consuming unpasteurised soft cheeses, and approximately three weeks prior to this presentation she had eaten a locally sourced soft cheese at a family gathering. There was no witnessed seizure activity, no rash, and no recent sick contacts with meningitis. The patient has been on prednisone 7.5 mg daily and methotrexate 15 mg weekly for rheumatoid arthritis for approximately four years. Her last rheumatology visit one month ago documented well-controlled disease. She has no history of prior CNS infection, neurosurgical procedures, or cerebrospinal fluid leak. On arrival to the ED she was febrile at 39.1 degrees Celsius, tachycardic, lethargic, and in moderate distress from photophobia and neck pain.

neurological_exam.additional: Moderate nuchal rigidity present; passive neck flexion produces significant resistance and patient moans with discomfort. Kernig sign positive bilaterally with resistance and pain on knee extension from 90 degrees hip flexion. Brudzinski sign positive with involuntary lower-extremity flexion on passive neck flexion. No petechial or purpuric rash on skin examination. No focal dermatological source of infection. Left knee prosthesis site without erythema, swelling, or warmth.
neurological_exam.coordination: Unable to reliably assess due to altered mental status.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, sluggishly reactive to light. No papilledema on fundoscopic exam. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Marked photophobia on penlight examination; patient grimaces and turns head away. Facial sensation intact bilaterally; face symmetric. Hearing grossly reduced bilaterally, attributed to baseline age-related presbycusis. Gag reflex intact. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to assess; patient too lethargic and unsteady to stand safely.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Lethargic, arousable to voice but falls asleep between questions. Oriented to name only; unable to state date, year, or location. Speech is slow and soft; language content is coherent when she can be kept awake. Does not follow commands; localises a painful stimulus with either hand. GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5). Daughter reports this represents a marked decline from baseline.
neurological_exam.motor: Moves all four extremities to noxious stimuli and localises with both arms; strength appears grossly 4/5 throughout but cannot be formally tested because she does not follow commands. No pronator drift. Tone normal except mild increase in lower extremities bilaterally, possibly age-related or medication-related.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally. Patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdraws symmetrically to pain in all four extremities. Formal sensory testing limited by encephalopathy.
